passages.title: Striped Chipmunk's Pockets
passages.text: "Of course," cried Peter. "I don't see how I came to forget that. I've laughed many times at Striped Chipmunk with those pockets stuffed with nuts or seeds until his head looked three times bigger than it does now. Those pockets must be very handy."

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What has Peter seen Striped Chipmunk stuff into his pockets?
choices: Nuts or seeds
Leaves and twigs
Berries and bugs
Pebbles and sand
question.evidence: pockets stuffed with nuts or seeds
question.explain: Peter remembers the pockets stuffed with nuts or seeds.

passages.title: Lightfoot's Antlers
passages.text: "Notice how long and fluffy the hair on that tail is," said Old Mother Nature. "Mrs. Lightfoot's is just like it, and this makes it very easy for her babies to follow her in the dark. When Lightfoot is feeding or simply walking about he carries it down, but when he is frightened and bounds away, up goes that white flag. Now look at his horns. They are not true horns. The latter are hollow, while these are not. Farmer Brown's cows have horns. Lightfoot has antlers. Just remember that. The so-called horns of all the Deer family are antlers and are not hollow. Notice how Lightfoot's curve forward with the branches or tines on the back side."

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: How are a deer's antlers different from a cow's horns?
choices: Antlers are much softer
Antlers grow on the nose
Antlers are not hollow
Antlers are always white
question.evidence: The so-called horns of all the Deer family are antlers and are not hollow.
question.explain: True horns are hollow, but antlers are not.

passages.title: The Otters' Slippery Slide
passages.text: Old Mother Nature smiled. "Little Joe Otter and his family are quite as fond of play as any of my children," said she. "They get a lot of fun out of life. One of their ways of playing is to make a slippery slide where the bank is steep and the water deep. In winter it is made of snow, but in summer it is made of mud. There they slide down, splash into the water, then climb up the bank and do it all over again. In winter they make their slippery slide where the water doesn't freeze, and they get just as much fun in winter as they do in summer."

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What do the otters do right after they splash into the water?
choices: Swim off to look for a fish dinner
Lie on the bank to dry in the sun
Dig a brand new slide in the mud
Climb up the bank and do it again
question.evidence: then climb up the bank and do it all over again
question.explain: They splash in, then climb up the bank and slide again.

passages.title: Bears of Another Color
passages.text: "You all see what a black coat Buster has," said Old Mother Nature. "Now I'm going to tell you something which may surprise you. Just as there are Red Foxes that are black, so there are Black Bears that are brown."

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What surprising fact does Old Mother Nature share?
choices: All bears turn black in winter
Some Black Bears have brown coats
Buster's coat is really dark red
Red Foxes and bears are cousins
question.evidence: so there are Black Bears that are brown
question.explain: She says some Black Bears are actually brown.

passages.title: Mrs. Grouse's Cloak
passages.text: "He didn't see me at all," chuckled Mrs. Grouse, as she settled down once more. "That is what comes of having a cloak so like the color of these nice brown leaves. He isn't the first one who has passed me without seeing me at all. It is better than trying to hide a nest, and I certainly am thankful to Old Mother Nature for the cloak she gave me. I wonder if every one of these twelve eggs will hatch. If they do, I certainly will have a family to be proud of."

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why did the passer-by not see Mrs. Grouse?
choices: She hid her nest deep in a log
She flew away just in time
Her feathers look like brown leaves
She was sitting very far away
question.evidence: having a cloak so like the color of these nice brown leaves
question.explain: Her brown "cloak" blends in with the leaves around her.

passages.title: Sally Sly's Egg
passages.text: "Sally Sly," snapped Jenny Wren. "Sally Sly the Cowbird. I hoped she wouldn't disgrace the Old Orchard this year, but she has. When Mr. and Mrs. Chebec returned from getting their breakfast this morning they found one of Sally Sly's eggs in their nest. They are terribly upset, and I don't blame them. If I were in their place I simply would throw that egg out. That's what I'd do, I'd throw that egg out!"

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why are Mr. and Mrs. Chebec upset?
choices: A strange egg is in their nest
Someone broke their nest apart
Their own eggs are all missing
Jenny Wren moved into the nest
question.evidence: they found one of Sally Sly's eggs in their nest
question.explain: They found Sally Sly's egg in their own nest.

passages.title: A Head in the Doorway
passages.text: The chips were dropped and the head was thrust farther out. The sides and throat were a soft reddish-tan and on each side at the beginning of the bill was a black patch. The top of the head was gray and just at the back was a little band of bright red. There was no mistaking that head. It belonged to Yellow Wing the Flicker beyond a doubt.

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: How could the watcher tell whose head it was?
choices: By the song that it sang
By the shape of its nest
By how fast it was flying
By the colors on its head
question.evidence: The top of the head was gray and just at the back was a little band of bright red
question.explain: The colors and markings showed it was Yellow Wing the Flicker.

passages.title: Bully the Sparrow
passages.text: Bully the English Sparrow is a born fighter. He never is happier than when he is in the midst of a fight or a fuss of some kind. The fact that all his neighbors were against him didn't bother Bully in the least.

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Bully is "a born fighter." What does that mean?
choices: Someone born during a fight
Someone who loves to fight
Someone too small to fight
Someone who fights at night
question.evidence: He never is happier than when he is in the midst of a fight
question.explain: Bully is happiest when he is in a fight, so fighting is natural to him.

passages.title: Happy Jack's Missing Nuts
passages.text: Poor Happy Jack! Soon he came dancing along with another nut to put in the hollow of the old chestnut tree. When he peeped in and saw that all his big store of nuts had disappeared, he couldn't believe his own eyes. He put in one paw and felt all around but not a nut could he feel. Then he climbed in and sure enough, the hollow was empty.

source.name: Old Mother West Wind (Thornton W. Burgess, 1910)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What did Happy Jack do right after he felt around with his paw?
choices: He climbed into the hollow
He ran to tell his friends
He went to find more nuts
He began to cry and cry
question.evidence: Then he climbed in and sure enough, the hollow was empty.
question.explain: After feeling with his paw, he climbed right in.

passages.title: The Smiling Pool
passages.text: By and by Billy Mink came to the Smiling Pool. Here the Laughing Brook stopped and rested on its way to join the Big River. It stopped its noisy laughing and singing and just lay smiling and smiling in the warm sunshine. The little flowers on the bank leaned over and nodded to it. The beech tree, which was very old, sometimes dropped a leaf into it. The cat-tails kept their feet cool in the edge of it.

source.name: Old Mother West Wind (Thornton W. Burgess, 1910)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What is this paragraph mostly about?
choices: How Billy Mink learned to swim well
Why the old beech tree drops leaves
The calm pool and what is around it
A noisy race down to the Big River
question.evidence: just lay smiling and smiling in the warm sunshine
question.explain: It describes the quiet Smiling Pool and the flowers, tree and cat-tails by it.

passages.title: The Willful Little Breeze
passages.text: Pretty soon all were in the bag but one, a willful little Breeze, who was not quite ready to go home; he wanted to play just a little longer. He danced ahead of Old Mother West Wind. He kissed the sleepy daisies. He shook the nodding buttercups. He set all the little poplar leaves a dancing, too, and he wouldn't come into the big bag. So Old Mother West Wind closed the big bag and slung it over her shoulder. Then she started on towards her home behind the Purple Hills.

source.name: Old Mother West Wind (Thornton W. Burgess, 1910)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: One little Breeze is "willful." What does willful mean?
choices: Feeling very tired and sleepy
Being the biggest of them all
Being afraid of the dark hills
Doing just what it wants to do
question.evidence: he wanted to play just a little longer
question.explain: The Breeze does what it wants and will not come into the bag.

passages.title: Bumble the Bee's Gold
passages.text: "Matter enough," grumbled Bumble the Bee. "I've got to make a sack of honey, and as if that isn't enough, old Mother Nature has ordered me to carry a sack of gold from each flower I visit to the next flower I visit. If I don't I can get no honey. Buzz-buzz-buzz," grumbled Bumble the Bee.

source.name: Mother West Wind's Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1911)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What is the "sack of gold" Bumble carries from flower to flower?
choices: Real gold coins for Mother Nature
Yellow pollen from the flowers
Honey to feed the baby bees
Seeds to plant in the garden
question.evidence: carry a sack of gold from each flower I visit to the next flower I visit
question.explain: Bees carry yellow pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds.

passages.title: Reddy Fox Boasts
passages.text: Just then Reddy Fox began to boast, for Reddy Fox is a great boaster. "Pooh!" said Reddy Fox, "pooh! Anybody could jump if their legs were made for jumping. And what's the good of climbing trees anyway? Now I can run faster than anybody here--faster than anybody in the whole world!" said Reddy Fox, puffing himself out.

source.name: Mother West Wind's Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1911)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Reddy is "puffing himself out." What is he trying to do?
choices: Catch his breath after a run
Blow the leaves away
Look big and important
Get ready to jump high
question.evidence: Reddy Fox is a great boaster
question.explain: He is bragging, so he puffs himself up to look important.

passages.title: Bobby Coon's Mischief
passages.text: Bobby Coon had been out all night. You see Bobby Coon is very apt to get into mischief, and because usually it is safer to get into mischief under cover of the darkness Bobby Coon prefers the night wherein to go abroad. Not that Bobby Coon is really bad! Oh my, no! Everybody likes Bobby Coon. But he can no more keep out of mischief than a duck can keep out of water.

source.name: Mother West Wind's Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1911)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why does Bobby Coon like to go out at night?
choices: Mischief is safer in the dark
He can't see well in the sun
His friends play only at night
He likes to watch the stars
question.evidence: it is safer to get into mischief under cover of the darkness
question.explain: Mischief is safer when the darkness hides him.

passages.title: Peter Visits Grandfather Frog
passages.text: "I couldn't sleep all winter if I wanted to, and I wouldn't if I could, for there is too much fun to miss," muttered Peter, as he started for the Smiling Pool in search of Grandfather Frog. He found him sitting on his big lily-pad, but somehow Grandfather Frog didn't look as chipper and smart as usual. "He certainly is growing old," thought Peter. "He isn't as spry as he used to be. Seems as if he had grown old in the last two or three weeks. Too bad, too bad."

source.name: Mother West Wind 'How' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1916)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why does Peter say "Too bad, too bad"?
choices: He could not find the Smiling Pool
He wishes he could sleep all winter
Grandfather Frog was rude to him
He is sad that his friend seems old
question.evidence: He certainly is growing old
question.explain: Peter is sorry to see that Grandfather Frog looks old and tired.

passages.title: Be Content
passages.text: "Chug-a-rum!" said Grandfather Frog. "Chug-a-rum! Be content with the blessings you have got, Peter Rabbit. Be content with the blessings you have got. No good comes of wishing for things which it never was meant that you should have. It is a bad habit and it makes discontent."

source.name: Mother West Wind 'How' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1916)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What lesson does Grandfather Frog give Peter?
choices: Always ask for what you want
Be happy with what you have
Learn to swim like a frog
Wish hard and it comes true
question.evidence: Be content with the blessings you have got
question.explain: He tells Peter to be content with the blessings he has.

passages.title: Blacky the Crow
passages.text: "Caw, caw, caw, caw!" Blacky the Crow sat in the top of a tall tree and seemed trying to see just how much noise he could make with that harsh voice of his. Peter Rabbit peered out from the dear Old Briar-patch and frowned.

source.name: Mother West Wind 'How' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1916)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: How does Peter feel about Blacky's noise?
choices: He does not like it
He thinks it is music
He wants to join in
He is scared of it
question.evidence: Peter Rabbit peered out from the dear Old Briar-patch and frowned.
question.explain: Peter frowned, so the harsh noise bothered him.

passages.title: Folded Hands
passages.text: Happy Jack Squirrel sat with his hands folded across his white waistcoat. He is very fond of sitting with his hands folded that way. A little way from him sat Peter Rabbit. Peter was sitting up very straight, but his hands dropped right down in front. Happy Jack noticed it.

source.name: Mother West Wind 'Why' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1915)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: How was Peter Rabbit sitting?
choices: Lying down with his eyes shut
With hands folded on his vest
Very straight, hands dropped
Curled up in a tight ball
question.evidence: Peter was sitting up very straight, but his hands dropped right down in front.
question.explain: Peter sat up straight with his hands dropped down in front.

passages.title: A Funny Place for a House
passages.text: Johnny Chuck scratched his head thoughtfully. "It does seem a funny place," he admitted. "It certainly does seem a funny place. But then, Jerry Muskrat is a funny fellow. You know how much of the time he stays in the water. That seems funny to me. I suppose there is a reason for it, and probably there is a reason for building his house where it is. I've found that there is a reason for most things. Probably Jerry's great-great-grandfather built his house that way, and so Jerry does the same thing."

source.name: Mother West Wind 'Why' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1915)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What has Johnny Chuck found out about most things?
choices: Most things should be kept secret
Most houses belong in water
Most old ways are wrong ones
Most things happen for a reason
question.evidence: I've found that there is a reason for most things.
question.explain: Johnny says there is a reason for most things.

passages.title: Peter's Questions
passages.text: "Chug-a-rum!" said he. "You and your questions are a nuisance, Peter Rabbit, and I may as well get rid of you now as to have you keep coming down here and pestering me to death. Besides, any one who has to keep such a sharp watch for Reddy Fox as you do ought to know why he wears a red coat. If you'll promise to sit perfectly still and ask no foolish questions, I'll tell you the story."

source.name: Mother West Wind 'Why' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1915)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why does Grandfather Frog agree to tell the story?
choices: Because Peter gave him a fly
To make Peter stop pestering
To make Reddy Fox go away
Because he loves to tell tales
question.evidence: I may as well get rid of you now as to have you keep coming down here and pestering me to death
question.explain: He wants Peter to stop coming back and bothering him.

passages.title: The Rock in Svithjod
passages.text: HIGH Up in the North in the land called Svithjod, there stands a rock. It is a hundred miles high and a hundred miles wide. Once every thousand years a little bird comes to this rock to sharpen its beak.

source.name: The Story of Mankind (Hendrik Willem van Loon, 1921)
source.author: Hendrik Willem van Loon

question.q: How often does the little bird come to the rock?
choices: Once every hundred years
Every spring when snow melts
Once every thousand years
Every morning at sunrise
question.evidence: Once every thousand years a little bird comes to this rock
question.explain: The bird comes only once every thousand years.

passages.title: Drying the Clothes
passages.text: "When Mother Ambroisine hangs the clothes she has just washed on the line, what does she do it for? To dry the linen, to free it from the water with which it is saturated. Well, what becomes of this water, if you please?"

question.q: The wet linen is "saturated" with water. What does saturated mean?
choices: Holding lots of water
Dried out by the sun
Folded in a neat pile
Scrubbed with soap
question.evidence: to free it from the water with which it is saturated
question.explain: Saturated means full of water, so the clothes must be dried.

passages.title: The Parts of a Flower
passages.text: "Let us begin with the blossoms of the digitalis, which I spoke of yesterday. Here is one. It has, as you see, almost the form of a glove-finger, or better, of a long pointed cap. Emile could put one on to his little finger; there would be plenty of room. It is purplish-red in color. Inside, it has spots of dark red encircled with white. The red glove-finger rises from the center of a circle of five little leaves. These little leaves are also part of the flower. Together they form what is called the calyx. The rest, the red part, is called the corolla. Remember these words, which are new to you."

question.q: What is the "calyx" of this flower?
choices: The red part shaped like a glove
The dark red spots with white rings
The tall stem that holds it up
The ring of five little leaves
question.evidence: Together they form what is called the calyx.
question.explain: The five little leaves at the bottom of the flower form the calyx.

passages.title: The Snail's Tentacles
passages.text: "Right at the end of each long tentacle you see a little black point. It is an eye as complete as that of the horse and ox, in spite of its minute dimensions. What is necessary for making an eye, you are far from suspecting. It is so complicated I will not try to tell you. And yet it is all to be found in that little black point that is scarcely visible. That is not all: beside the eye is a nose, that is to say an organ especially sensitive to odors. The snail sees and smells with the tips of its long tentacles."

question.q: What is this paragraph mostly about?
choices: How a horse and an ox see things
What a snail's tentacles can do
Why snails move very slowly
How to make a tiny black eye
question.evidence: The snail sees and smells with the tips of its long tentacles.
question.explain: It explains the eye and nose at the tips of a snail's tentacles.

passages.title: Things That Seem to Move
passages.text: "Without being able to explain it to myself well," returned Emile, "I see that it is so. We move and we think we see the other things moving. The faster we go, the faster the other things seem to go."

question.q: What happens to other things when we go faster?
choices: Other things seem to move faster
Other things seem to stand still
Other things seem to get bigger
Other things seem to slow down
question.evidence: The faster we go, the faster the other things seem to go.
question.explain: Emile says the faster we go, the faster other things seem to go.

passages.title: Picciola
passages.text: One fine morning in spring, Char-ney was taking his walk in the yard. He was counting the paving stones, as he had done a thousand times before. All at once he stopped. What had made that little mound of earth between two of the stones?

question.q: Why did Charney stop all at once?
choices: He heard a loud bang
He felt too tired to go on
He saw something new
He lost his count of stones
question.evidence: What had made that little mound of earth between two of the stones?
question.explain: He noticed a little mound of earth that had not been there before.

passages.title: Grace Darling
passages.text: In a few minutes they were ready. They set off in the heavy lighthouse boat. Grace pulled one oar, and her father the other, and they made straight toward the wreck. But it was hard rowing against such a sea, and it seemed as though they would never reach the place.

question.q: Why did it seem they would never reach the wreck?
choices: Their little boat had a leak
They had only one oar to use
A thick fog hid the wreck
The waves made it hard to row
question.evidence: it was hard rowing against such a sea
question.explain: The rough sea made rowing very hard.

passages.title: Bruce and the Spider
passages.text: As he lay thinking, he saw a spider over his head, making ready to weave her web. He watched her as she toiled slowly and with great care. Six times she tried to throw her frail thread from one beam to another, and six times it fell short.

question.q: How many times did the spider's thread fall short?
choices: Three times
Six times
Seven times
Ten times
question.evidence: six times it fell short
question.explain: The spider tried six times, and six times the thread fell short.

passages.title: Androclus and the Lion
passages.text: After a while a great noise woke him up. A lion had come into the cave, and was roaring loudly. Androclus was very much afraid, for he felt sure that the beast would kill him. Soon, however, he saw that the lion was not angry, but that he limped as though his foot hurt him.

question.q: Why did Androclus soon feel less afraid?
choices: The lion fell fast asleep
A friend came to help him
The lion seemed hurt, not angry
He found a way out of the cave
question.evidence: he saw that the lion was not angry, but that he limped as though his foot hurt him
question.explain: The lion was limping in pain, not angry.

passages.title: Paul Revere Waits
passages.text: When night came, Paul Revere was at the riverside with his horse. He looked over toward Boston. He knew where the old North Church stood, but he could not see much in the darkness.

question.q: Why could Paul Revere not see much?
choices: Night had made it dark
Fog covered the river
His horse was in the way
Trees blocked his view
question.evidence: he could not see much in the darkness
question.explain: It was night, so he could not see much in the darkness.

passages.title: Benjamin's Shopping Trip
passages.text: As Benjamin ran down the street, he wondered what he should buy. Should he buy candy? He hardly knew how it tasted. Should he buy a pretty toy? If he had been the only child in the family, things might have been different. But there were fourteen boys and girls older than he, and two little sisters who were younger.

question.q: Why might Benjamin hardly know how candy tasted?
choices: He never liked sweet things at all
No shops in his town sold candy
His mother said candy was bad
There were many kids to share with
question.evidence: there were fourteen boys and girls older than he
question.explain: With so many children in the family, there was little left for treats.

passages.title: The Two Wreaths
passages.text: "One of these wreaths." said the queen, "is made of flowers plucked from your garden. The other is made of artificial flowers, shaped and colored by a skillful artist. Now, tell me, O King, which is the true, and which is the false?"

question.q: What are "artificial flowers"?
choices: Flowers picked that morning
Flowers made by a person
Flowers grown in the shade
Flowers that smell sweet
question.evidence: artificial flowers, shaped and colored by a skillful artist
question.explain: Artificial flowers are made by a person, not grown.

passages.title: The Bag of Gold
passages.text: The gardener answered: "A year ago, as I was spading in my garden, I saw something fall at the foot of a palm tree. I ran to pick it up and was surprised to find that it was a bag full of bright gold pieces. I said to myself, 'This money must belong to our master, Al Mansour. Some large bird has stolen it from his palace.'"

question.q: What kind of person does the gardener seem to be?
choices: Honest and true
Greedy and selfish
Lazy and careless
Rude and unkind
question.evidence: This money must belong to our master, Al Mansour.
question.explain: He found gold and thought first of who it belonged to.

passages.title: The wise man
passages.text: Once upon a time, there was a man who thought that the youth were wiser than their elders. He even bragged about it before his wife. He said to her, "I am wiser than your father." His wife disagreed with him, but he would not listen to her. One day when the wife went to see her parents, she told her father about how his son-in-law claims to be wiser than him because he is younger. The old man sent his daughter back to ask her husband if he still held the same view.

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Cornelius Wekunya
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: What did the man brag about to his wife?
choices: That he was richer than her father
That he was stronger than her father
That he was wiser than her father
That he was older than her father
question.evidence: I am wiser than your father.
question.explain: He said, "I am wiser than your father."

passages.title: Nonkungu and the imbulu
passages.text: Once upon a time there was a poor man and his wife. They had only one child, a girl. The child's name was Nonkungu. Her parents loved Nonkungu very much. One day her parents decided to send her to stay with her rich Uncle Mtonyama. Nonkungu's mother made a special skirt with ribbon, buttons and beads. She also made a beautiful bead necklace for Nonkungu. Then she sent her off to her uncle's village.

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Alan Kenyon, Viv Kenyon
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

choices: Baked bread for the long trip
Wrote a letter to the uncle
Sold their cow for some money
Made her a skirt and necklace
question.evidence: She also made a beautiful bead necklace for Nonkungu. Then she sent her off
question.explain: She made a skirt and a necklace, then sent Nonkungu off.

passages.title: Elephant and Chameleon
passages.text: Once upon a time in a big palace, there lived a king and his beautiful daughter, the princess. Elephant lived in a house on one side of the palace. Chameleon lived on the other side. At this time, there was a terrible drought across the land. The king had an idea and called his two neighbours to the palace.

source.author: Stella Badaru
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

A long time with no rain
A cold time with lots of snow
A loud party at a palace
question.evidence: there was a terrible drought across the land
question.explain: A drought is a long time without rain.

passages.title: Clever cat
passages.text: In my village lives Mister Kiio. Mister Kiio has a cat with black and white spots called Safi. When Mister Kiio goes to work, he leaves the door open. Safi sits in the doorway to watch over Mister Kiio's house. When the neighbour's dog comes close, Safi stares at him and shows her nails.

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Ursula Nafula
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

choices: A dog that is friends with a cat
A man who loses his front door
A cat who watches over a house
A cat that learns to paint spots
question.evidence: Safi sits in the doorway to watch over Mister Kiio's house.
question.explain: Safi guards Mister Kiio's house while he is at work.

passages.title: Amazing Daisy
passages.text: "Daisy, we can all flap our wings but it's very difficult for chickens to fly," Mama told her. Daisy wouldn't give up. Every day she practised by herself, flapping her wings. Flap, flap, flap, she would flap her wings but she couldn't lift off the ground. While she practised, she imagined herself flying high into the sky and looking at the chickens below. She imagined herself flying past the sparrows and past the swallows. "Wow!" the birds would say. "A chicken that can fly!"

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Nozizwe Herero
source.note: Excerpt from the story. Illustrations not included.

question.evidence: Daisy wouldn't give up.
question.explain: Daisy practises flying every day and does not give up.

passages.title: The puppy that did not bark!!!
passages.text: As soon as she got up in the morning she begged her father, "Daddy, please, please get me a pup." Her father said "Sure Rinku, as soon as you grow a little older." One evening on the way back from school, Rinku heard some noise in the bushes near her house. She ran towards the noise and found a little brown puppy under the bushes. Rinku was very excited. She carefully picked up the small furry bundle and carried it home. She kept it in a small box in the garden. This was her big secret.

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Uma Balamurali
source.note: Excerpt from the story. Illustrations not included.

Her father said she was too young
question.evidence: as soon as you grow a little older
question.explain: Her father had said to wait until she was older.

passages.title: Gulli's Box of Things
passages.text: "What's wrong Grandpa, why are you not reading the newspaper?" asked Gulli one morning. "Oh dear, I broke my reading glasses, and I can't read anything without them," said Grandpa. "Ah, don't you worry, Grandpa. Let me go and get my box of things." Gulli ran out fast, and came back with his little brown box.

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Anupama Ajinkya Apte
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.explain: Gulli ran out and came back with his box of things.

passages.title: Daddy's Mo
passages.text: Anu likes many things about Daddy. She likes the bright paper lanterns he makes, the crisp onion pakodas he fries and the cute tortoise he makes out of paper. Besides, he climbs the stairs with a hop, and wrestles with Uncle for fun. When guests come over, he always makes them laugh. Anu likes all these things about Daddy. But do you know what Anu likes most of all? Daddy's moustache!

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Madhuri Purandare
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included. Translated by Sai Keskar.

His onion pakodas
His funny jokes
question.evidence: Daddy's moustache!
question.explain: Anu likes his moustache most of all.

passages.title: Jaggee's mornings
passages.text: Every weekday morning Jaggee's alarm clock rings at 5 o'clock and every weekday morning he tries to ignore it. "I do not like mornings!" groans Jaggee. But Jaggee has school. He hides under the blankets and pretends that it isn't really morning. He complains. He says nasty things about mornings. "Most of the days I fall back to sleep for a few minutes!", Jaggee says.

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Sandhya Sridhar
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.evidence: He complains. He says nasty things about mornings.
question.explain: To groan is to make an unhappy sound, like a complaint.

passages.title: Hot Tea and Warm Rugs
passages.text: Amma says people in Gujarat have a Ponkh festival in winter. Farmers roast bundles of millet on coal stoves. Everyone eats the fresh, green, plump and tender beads of millet grains called ponkh. I wore a bright blue sweater to the fair. There were many stalls all along the road. Manu wanted to go on the merry-go-round. I wanted to buy grandma a warm, soft shawl.

source.author: Mala Kumar, Manisha Chaudhry
source.note: Excerpt from the story. Illustrations not included.

question.evidence: tender beads of millet grains called ponkh
question.explain: Ponkh is the fresh, green millet grains people eat.

passages.title: My Juggling Granny
passages.text: Grannies come in many sizes, And they give us funny surprises! Did you know my granny juggles? With her, I like to snuggle! A great spotter of things is she, She's not one to let things be! An expert at tossing everything in sight, People around get quite a fright!

source.author: Mala Kumar, Manisha Chaudhry
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included. Translated by Mala Kumar, Manisha Chaudhry.

question.explain: She tosses everything in sight, which surprises people.

passages.title: Sakima's song
passages.text: Sakima lived with his parents and his four year old sister. They lived on a rich man's land. Their grass-thatched hut was at the end of a row of trees. When Sakima was three years old, he fell sick and lost his sight. Sakima was a talented boy. Sakima did many things that other six year old boys did not do. For example, he could sit with older members of the village and discuss important matters.

source.author: Ursula Nafula
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.evidence: When Sakima was three years old, he fell sick and lost his sight.
question.explain: At three, Sakima fell sick and lost his sight.

passages.title: A Tiny Seed: The Story of Wangari Maathai
passages.text: Wangari was a clever child and couldn't wait to go to school. But her mother and father wanted her to stay and help them at home. When she was seven years old, her big brother persuaded her parents to let her go to school. She liked to learn! Wangari learnt more and more with every book she read. She did so well at school that she was invited to study in the United States of America. Wangari was excited! She wanted to know more about the world.

source.name: Storybooks Canada
source.author: Nicola Rijsdijk
source.note: Excerpt from the story. Illustrations not included.

question.explain: Doing well at school led to an invitation to study in the USA.

passages.title: Magozwe
passages.text: In the busy city of Nairobi, far away from a caring life at home, lived a group of homeless boys. They welcomed each day just as it came. On one morning, the boys were packing their mats after sleeping on cold pavements. To chase away the cold they lit a fire with rubbish. Among the group of boys was Magozwe. He was the youngest.

source.name: Storybooks Canada
source.author: Lesley Koyi
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.explain: It tells about a group of homeless boys starting a cold day in Nairobi.
